name: glám dícenn

attributes.attribute: Irish ritual posture for casting a curse
required standing on one leg with one arm out and one eye closed
king cursed through the glám dícenn
sacred vows broken by King Conaire

sources: Monaghan, Patricia. The Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore. Checkmark Books, 2008.
text: In ancient Ireland a bard or druid used a ritual posture to cast a poet's execration. The practice is known as the glám dícenn. The Irish word pairs glám, meaning satire or lampoon, with a verb form meaning to destroy outright. The caster stood on one leg in a crane-like pose. He closed one eye and stretched out one arm. The pose was not theatre. The ritual carried weight as a weapon of war. It could raise blisters on the target's face. It could cost the target his life. Society at every level shunned a man once the curse was laid. The form compares with the hija wielded by early Arab poets. A Hag used the glám dícenn against King Conaire in Da Derga's Hostel. She cursed him for breaking his sacred vows, called geis.

okr.objective: Present the glám dícenn as a poet's execration with a defined ritual posture and real social force.
key_results: A bard or druid cast the glám dícenn from a one-leg, one-arm, one-eye pose.
The ritual acted as a weapon of war that could maim or kill the target.
Society shunned the victim at every level, in the manner of the hija curse.
